extracted.intended_audience: writers, poets, artists, and students of aesthetics seeking to produce the sublime in literature or visual/auditory art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to create the aesthetic effect called 'the sublime' by evoking terror-like tension, using scale, unity, repetition, contrast (darkness/blackness), and controlled pain/strain in sensory or imagined experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime grounded in terror/pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever produces an 'unnatural tension, contraction, or violent emotion of the nerves'—a mode of terror or pain—will be productive of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pain and terror act similarly on body and mind (pain via body, terror via mind suggesting danger). Examples: convulsive agitations in weak subjects; mimicry (Campanella) where adopting gestures excites corresponding passions. Use stimuli that induce bodily tension or the idea of danger to build the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled/moderated pain yields delight (delightful horror)
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain mode of pain or terror, when not actually noxious and not carried to violence, can produce delight — a 'delightful horror' distinct from ordinary pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for non-noxious intensity: emotions like astonishment (highest), awe, reverence, and respect are subordinate degrees. The effect belongs to self-preservation and is strongest when terror-like impressions are present but not overwhelming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of great visual dimensions (vastness) to strain the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual objects great in dimensions produce sublimity because the eye (retina) must take in many points or traverse vast space quickly, producing strain/tension akin to pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke scale and vastness (e.g., enormous bodies, extensive spaces) so the sensory organs are worked up; the effect derives from either many simultaneous impressions or the rapid motion of the eye across great extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and simplicity requisite to vastness
rubrics_metrics.description: For vastness to be sublime it must present unity — 'one, simple and entire' — because the mind cannot attend diligently to many distinct little objects at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a single, uniform, uninterrupted object or composition (shape, disposition, colouring). Varied small parts prevent the continuous tension necessary for the sublime; unity detains the eye and mind rather than letting them quickly find termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial infinite: succession of uniform great parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A uniform succession of large similar parts (the 'artificial infinite')—in sight or sound—creates expectation and repeated tension that builds toward the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated, similar elements (e.g., a long colonnade of identical pillars, repeated musical strokes) so each repetition increases tension by expectation and surprise, accumulating toward the verge of pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of vibrations/impressions (consistency required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vibrations or impressions must be similar and repeated; variation interrupts the build-up and prevents the sublime from being carried beyond the number of actual impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure successive stimuli maintain the same character/direction (analogy: a pendulum pushed repeatedly in the same direction achieves greater amplitude). Alternation or dissimilarity acts as rest/relief and reduces effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession and repetition produce expectation and surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated strokes or events create expectation (which itself causes tension); when the event returns, surprise further increases tension — both aid the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure sensory or narrative occurrences with an interval that creates expectation but uncertainty about exact timing (e.g., successive cannon fire); exploit the interplay of anticipation and arrival to escalate feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession in visual objects — colonnade example
rubrics_metrics.description: A row of uniform pillars viewed so the eye 'shoots along' them produces repeated impulses that violently rouse the organ of sight, producing a grand or sublime conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In visual composition (or descriptive writing), arrange uniform elements in a straight line or repetition that allows the observer/reader's attention to move along and be repeatedly impressed; avoid alternating forms that relax the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast: bare uniformity vs repeated parts (detain the eye)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long bare wall, though vast, is less sublime than a colonnade because the eye arrives at its termination quicker and is not detained by repeated similar impulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes so repetition detains attention rather than offering a single immediate sweep; repetition of parts is more effective than single vast uniform surfaces for sustained sublime effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-dangerous things can produce terror-like passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects not actually dangerous may produce a passion like terror through how they affect the finer organs (eye, ear) or by associated ideas of danger, and thus serve as sources of the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ stimuli that mimic the bodily effects of terror (strain, tension) without real harm — e.g., vastness, sudden shifts, intense sounds — so the audience experiences terror-like emotion safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darkness and blackness as means to the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Darkness (and blackness as partial darkness) can be naturally terrible because utter darkness makes safety uncertain and can physically strain ocular parts (pupil/iris) producing painful sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use darkness or black elements to create uncertainty and bodily strain in perception; contrast of light/dark and sudden introductions of darkness can produce convulsive reactions and imaginative terror (evidence: anecdote of a boy newly sighted reacting to black objects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackness causes sudden relaxation/convulsive recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Black patches amid coloured surroundings act as vacuities that, when the eye falls on them after tension, cause sudden relaxation followed by convulsive spring — a shock contributing to the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place dark/black areas beside active coloured fields to create abrupt sensory change; exploit the startle effect produced by unexpected relaxation and recovery in the senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise/labour as necessary for the finer organs and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical or mental exercise (a mode of pain) is necessary to keep the coarser and finer organs in proper tone; adequate 'labour' readies the organs that imagination uses and helps produce sublime effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage engagement/effort in attention or sensory work (in composition or performance) to stimulate the faculties; over-relaxation leads to melancholy and diminishes the capacity for sublime responses, while moderate strain sharpens perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid petty variation and teazing actions that relax rather than strain
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent petty changes (colours, shapes) provide relief/relaxation to the organs and prevent the uniform vigorous labour allied to strong pain that causes the sublime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from interrupting uniform sequences with trivial variety; small, teasing variations fatigue and weaken the sensory effect instead of building it.
